title: Quantum Complexity Dynamics for Disjoint Subsystems
authors: Yale Fan, Nicholas Hunter-Jones, Andreas Karch, Minju Kum, Shivan Mittal
abstract: Quantum complexity has emerged as a natural probe of chaos, thermalization, and the black hole interior on timescales long after local observables have equilibrated. However, its time evolution has been studied almost exclusively in subsystems confined to a single connected region. We show, using complementary tools from holography and random quantum circuits, that noncontiguous subsystems composed of multiple disjoint regions give rise to qualitatively new physics compared to the contiguous case. First, at finite temperature, a subsystem occupying less than half of the total system can carry high complexity at late times, even as the complexity of its larger complement remains low. This inversion of the usual hierarchy is intrinsically thermal: it vanishes in the infinite-temperature limit, which is the regime modeled by random quantum circuits. Second, if a subsystem's complexity equilibrates at an early time, then fragmenting it into $m$ disjoint components can further reduce this timescale by a factor of $m$, a phenomenon we exhibit in both holography and random quantum circuits. These results not only sharpen the correspondence between geometric and computational notions of complexity, but also motivate the search for novel complexity phenomena in quantum dynamics.
summary: This paper explores quantum complexity dynamics in systems where the subsystems are not connected. Using both holographic models and random quantum circuits, the authors demonstrate counterintuitive effects, such as a smaller, fragmented subsystem carrying high complexity while a larger one remains simple at finite temperatures. This work sharpens the link between geometric structure and computational complexity in quantum dynamics.
main_problem: The paper investigates quantum complexity dynamics, focusing specifically on how the complexity evolves in noncontiguous (disjoint) subsystems, which is expected to reveal physics beyond the standard connected region analysis.
main_result: The study shows that at finite temperature, a smaller, noncontiguous subsystem can exhibit exponentially large complexity while its larger complement remains simple, an effect that vanishes in the infinite-temperature limit.
method: The authors employ complementary theoretical tools from holographic duality (AdS/CFT) and the analysis of random quantum circuits to calculate quantum complexity.
model_or_system: The models include a CFT on a spatial circle in the thermofield double state (holography) and random quantum circuits on qudits. The analysis compares the complexity of disjoint subsystems A and B.
key_observables: Quantum Complexity, Entanglement Entropy, and the Ryu–Takayanagi (RT) surface area/volume.
important_parameters: Finite temperature ($ eta$ finite) vs. infinite temperature ($ eta 	o 0$); the number of disjoint components ($m$).
main_assumptions: The holographic setup assumes identical subsystems on both sides to model the symmetry of the thermofield double state.
figures_summary: Figures 1 and 2 illustrate candidate RT surface configurations and the implications of the black hole location relative to the entanglement wedge.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the holographic complexity for $m=2$ and $m=3$ disjoint intervals, generalizes to arbitrary $m$ to derive the complexity collapse time, and then presents the analogous results using random quantum circuits.
why_interesting: The findings provide novel insights into how geometric properties (disjointness) can drastically alter the expected thermalization and complexity dynamics of quantum systems, which is relevant for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in many-body systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two candidate RT surface configurations. All intervals have size < ℓ/2. Left: the “B caps” have smaller area, and the connected entanglement wedge of A (colored in red) contains the wormhole despite that ℓA < ℓ/2. Right: the “A caps” have smaller area, and the entanglement wedge of A does not contain the wormhole.

Figure 2: The case where the complementary subsystem B contains an interval of size > ℓ/2, namely B2. Left: the “B caps” have smaller area. Right: the “A caps” have smaller area. In either case, the entanglement wedge of A does not contain the wormhole.

Figure 3: Lower and upper bounds for rB1/B as functions of p, where rA1/A = 1/2. The blue line is the lower bound. The yellow, green, and orange lines are the upper bounds for ℓ/β = 10−10, ℓ/β = 1, and ℓ/β = 5, respectively. The allowed regions in the (p, rB1/B) parameter space are colored accordingly. For example, when ℓ/β = 1, the allowed region is the union of the green and orange regions. As the temperature increases, the allowed region shrinks.
